title: Weight tends to vary as the cube of linear dimensions during growth

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Weight tends to vary as the cube of linear dimensions during growth

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Whatever the law of increase in a linear dimension, volume and therefore weight tend to vary as the cube of linear dimensions, which mainly (though not wholly) explains why the human weight curve differs in shape from the stature curve.

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: W \propto L^3 whatever the law of growth L(t)

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: whatever be the law of increment in a linear dimension, the law of increase in volume, and therefore in weight, will be that these latter magnitudes tend to vary as the cubes of the linear dimensions.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter III, “The Rate of Growth”; topic “Rate of growth in man”. Scope: growing humans (and organisms generally)

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: W \propto L^3 whatever the law of growth L(t)

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch03-07: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.90

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Large open anthropometric datasets directly contain the variables across growth. A standard allometric regression cleanly tests the cubic tendency and quantifies the stated qualifications.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit log body weight against log stature through growth and test whether the exponent is near three, with deviations attributable to changing shape or density. An exponent materially different from three or systematic residual trends would refute strict cubic similarity.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Human proportions and tissue composition change with age.

Repeated cross-sections are not individual trajectories.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Paired height and weight through human growth are among the most completely published biological measurements, and the cube-law regression is immediate. The claim is already hedged as a tendency and as the main rather than the only reason the weight curve differs from the stature curve, and those hedges can be scored by how much of the curve difference the cubic term removes. That is a direct test with existing open data.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit log weight on log height through childhood and adolescence, and compare the weight curve with the cube of the stature curve. A slope near 3, and an alignment of the two curves after that cubic transformation, would support the claim; a slope far from 3, or a residual shape difference that the cube does not remove, would count against the claim that the cube is the main reason the curves differ.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value: Changing proportions and body composition move the exponent off 3, which the claim already allows as not the whole explanation.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: Across human growth, body weight scales approximately as the cube of stature (log-log slope near 3), and cubing the stature-versus-age curve removes most of the difference in shape between the stature curve and the weight curve.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: NHANES DEMO+BMX 2007-2018 merged on SEQN; examined persons under 20 yr with measured weight and stature (recumbent length < 24 months, standing height otherwise), n = 23540. OLS of log10 weight on log10 stature across individuals (95% CI from the regression standard error; RMA slope as sensitivity), and the same regression on the 240 monthly medians (age-median curve). Monthly median stature H(t) and weight W(t) were normalised by their mean over months 228-239 and the discrepancy D(p) = mean_t |W(t) - H(t)^p| computed for p = 1..4 and on a 0.01 grid to find the best exponent. Slopes by age window (0-2, 2-10, 10-20, 2-20 yr) are reported descriptively.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered, on pooled NHANES 2007-2018 individuals aged 0-19.99 yr with measured weight and stature (recumbent length < 24 months, standing height >= 24 months), sexes pooled with sex-specific values reported. (1) Cube tendency: the OLS slope b of log10(weight) on log10(stature) over all individuals satisfies 2.5 <= b <= 3.5 (95% CI reported; reduced-major-axis slope reported as sensitivity), and the same slope fitted to the age-median curve (monthly median weight vs monthly median stature, 0-19 yr) also lies in [2.5, 3.5]. (2) 'Mainly explains the curve difference': with monthly medians H(t), W(t) normalised to their 19-yr values, define D(p) = mean over months of |W(t)/W(19) - (H(t)/H(19))^p|. Supports if D(3)/D(1) <= 0.5, i.e. cubing the stature curve removes at least half of the discrepancy between the stature and weight curves. Both (1) and (2) must hold for 'supports'.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Refutes if the individual-level slope b lies outside [2.0, 4.0], or if D(3)/D(1) > 1 (cubing makes the curves less alike). Mixed if b is in [2.0, 2.5) or (3.5, 4.0], or if the slope is in range but 0.5 < D(3)/D(1) <= 1 (the cube explains some but not most of the difference).

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: log-log OLS exponent of weight on stature, individuals aged 0-19

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Thompson's 'linear dimension' is stature, 'weight' is body mass; 'tend to vary as the cube' is read as a log-log allometric exponent within 0.5 of 3 (his own hedge). The second half of the claim, that cubic scaling 'mainly (though not wholly)' explains why the weight curve differs in shape from the stature curve, is read as: the cube of the normalised stature curve is at least twice as close to the normalised weight curve as the stature curve itself. Humans only; the parenthetical extension to organisms generally is not tested. Cross-sectional data, modern US population.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
NHANES Demographic Variables and Sample Weights (DEMO), cycles 2007-2008 to 2017-2018

NHANES Body Measures (BMX), cycles 2007-2008 to 2017-2018

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
The two halves of the claim come apart. The allometric exponent across growth is 2.41 (CI 2.40-2.42; curve-level 2.46; RMA 2.50), below the pre-registered [2.5, 3.5] window, so weight does not vary as the cube of stature in the strict sense: proportions and composition change with age (window exponents 2.10 at 0-2 yr, 2.36 at 2-10 yr, 3.10 at 10-20 yr).

The second clause passes clearly: cubing the normalised stature curve removes 80% of its discrepancy from the normalised weight curve (D(3)/D(1) = 0.196; best exponent for curve shape 3.35), so the cubic relation does 'mainly, though not wholly' explain why the weight curve differs in shape from the stature curve, as Thompson said.

The exponent that best matches curve shapes (3.35) differs from the log-log slope (2.41) because the normalised-curve comparison weights late ages (where W/W19 is near 1) differently from a log-log fit dominated by infancy and childhood; both numbers are reported.

Cross-sectional data from a modern US population with high adolescent adiposity, which raises the 10-20 yr exponent; a leaner historical population would likely give a lower overall exponent, not a higher one.

Only the human part of the scope was tested; the parenthetical 'organisms generally' was not.

fields.value: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
